Foreign guests' seasons in Europe's regions — findings¶

Summary¶

This notebook backs the page Peaks and Plateaus: Europe's Foreign Tourism Rhythms (index.html). The page — and so this notebook — looks at foreign guests' nights only, along two dimensions: how many foreign nights a region has (volume) and how concentrated they are in time (months needed to reach 75% of the year's foreign nights). Domestic guests appear only as the comparison in section 4. Part 1 comes first as context: all guests and the foreign share of nights, not shown on the page.

Question Answer Section Page
1. How large is foreign tourism, and where? 62% of the EU-27's 952 million platform nights in 2025 were by foreign guests (67% in 2019). Country shares range from 29% (Germany) to over 95% (Malta, Iceland, Liechtenstein). Foreign nights are concentrated: the mainly-foreign regions (≥ 70% foreign) hold 64% of them, the ten largest regions 36%. Since 2019 domestic stays grew faster (+112% vs +73%), so the foreign share fell in 26 of 31 countries. 1.1–1.2 (context, not on the page)
2. Where and when do foreign guests stay? 609 million foreign nights in 2025 (31 countries), 44% of them in June–August. They are concentrated: the 43 regions with over 3 million foreign nights hold 73% of them. A typical region needs 7 months to reach 75% of its foreign nights (an even year needs 9); the Croatian coast needs 3, Madrid, Budapest, Berlin, Brussels and Bucharest 9. Large destinations are not systematically more seasonal. 2.1–2.5 map, country grid, notes
3. What seasonal cycles are there? Five patterns of foreign demand in the 255 regions with enough foreign nights: strong summer (58 regions, mostly coast and countryside), summer (131), summer + winter shoulder (5, not a firm group), winter-based (18, mountains) and mild or no season (43, cities). 3.1–3.3 chapter 2
4. Do foreign guests sharpen the local season? Depending on foreign guests does not make a region seasonal: foreign share and seasonality are only loosely related, and the data show no causal link. Foreign guests' timing matters more: it makes the year clearly sharper in 105 of 254 regions and clearly flatter in 27. The typical effect is small (+0.015 Gini) but about +0.06 where foreign guests are ≥ 70% of nights. They smooth the year where domestic guests crowd into August (Spain's coasts, Algarve, Sicilia). 4.1–4.4 chapter 3
5. What explains seasonality? Geography and country: rural and coastal regions have shorter foreign seasons. Neither foreign volume nor foreign share adds anything once these are known. 5.1–5.2 (typical geography row)

Limitations are at the end (Conclusions). Appendix A checks that every number in the text still matches the data; Appendix B checks that the data embedded in index.html match the dataset and the calculations here.

Setup¶

Loads data/ready/tour_ce_omn12_indices.csv (made by Stage 2 Indices.ipynb) and checks that the seasonality functions here give the same values as the indices notebook. Unless stated otherwise: 2025, NUTS 2 regions (259, including the Extra-Regio Mount Athos, as on the page), foreign guests. Seasonality indices (Gini, patterns, timing effect) need at least 10,000 nights in the series (VolumeOK = 1); months to 75% (Season75) is given for every region. Gini differences under 0.02–0.03 and changes of one month in Season75 are within a region's normal year-to-year movement (indices notebook, A3; section 2.4 here).

import json
import re

import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 200)
pd.set_option("display.width", 200)

# The dataset with all indices, made by the indices notebook (step 2). Only truly empty cells are missing values.
df = pd.read_csv("data/ready/tour_ce_omn12_indices.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig", keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])

MONTH_NAMES = ["January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June", "July", "August",
               "September", "October", "November", "December"]
df["Month"] = pd.Categorical(df["Month"], categories=MONTH_NAMES + ["Total"], ordered=True)
COUNTRIES = df["Country"].unique().tolist()                    # Eurostat's order
df["Country"] = pd.Categorical(df["Country"], categories=COUNTRIES, ordered=True)

# Text columns with a natural order become ordered categories (tables and charts follow that order).
PATTERNS = ["Strong summer season", "Summer season", "Summer season + winter shoulder", "Winter-based seasons", "Mild or no season"]
CATEGORIES = {
    "ForeignGroup": ["Mainly domestic", "Mixed", "Mainly foreign"],
    "SeasonShape": ["One season", "Two seasons", "No clear season"],
    "SeasonPattern": PATTERNS,
    "ForeignTimingClass": ["Reduces", "No clear effect", "Adds"],
    "UrbanGroup": ["Predominantly urban", "Intermediate", "Predominantly rural"],
    "CoastalGroup": ["Non-coastal", "Partly coastal", "Predominantly coastal"],
    "InlandMountainGroup": ["Non-inland mountain", "Partly inland mountain", "Predominantly inland mountain"],
    "IslandGroup": ["Non-island", "Partly island", "Predominantly island"]}
for col, cats in CATEGORIES.items():
    assert set(df[col].dropna().unique()) <= set(cats), col  # no unexpected labels
    df[col] = pd.Categorical(df[col], categories=cats, ordered=True)

# Series = region x year x guest group; 'wide' = its 12 months as columns (for the calculations that need months).
KEY_SERIES = ["NUTSCode", "Year", "ResidenceCountry"]
monthly = df["Month"] != "Total"
wide = df[monthly].pivot_table(index=KEY_SERIES, columns="Month", values="Value", observed=True).reindex(columns=MONTH_NAMES)
flags = df[monthly].pivot_table(index=KEY_SERIES, columns="Month", values="Prc75Flag", observed=True).reindex(columns=MONTH_NAMES)
volume_ok = df[~monthly].set_index(KEY_SERIES)["VolumeOK"].reindex(wide.index).eq(1)
T = 12
THETA = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(T) / T

# The seasonality measures, as defined and tested in the indices notebook (A1, A2, A4).
def gini(y):
    """Gini index of 12 monthly values (0 = flat year, 0.917 = all nights in one month)."""
    y = np.asarray(y, float); rank = np.empty(T); rank[np.argsort(y, kind="stable")] = np.arange(1, T + 1)
    F = rank / T
    return 2 * np.mean((y - y.mean()) * (F - F.mean())) / y.mean()
def s_r(y):
    """S_R (Lo Magno et al. 2017): minimum moving effort around the calendar, 0-1."""
    y = np.asarray(y, float); d = np.cumsum(y - y.mean())
    return np.abs(d - np.median(d)).sum() / (3 * y.sum())
def pcd_centre(y):
    """PCD (0-1) and season centre (1.0 = January ... 12.99) of 12 monthly values."""
    y = np.asarray(y, float); cx, sy = (y * np.cos(THETA)).sum(), (y * np.sin(THETA)).sum()
    return np.hypot(cx, sy) / y.sum(), (np.arctan2(sy, cx) % (2 * np.pi)) / (2 * np.pi) * T + 1
def top75(y):
    """Busiest months that together reach 75% of the year (month positions 0-11), as Season75 / Prc75Flag:
    take months from the busiest down while the running total is below 75%; months tied with the last one also count."""
    y = np.asarray(y, float); out, cum = [], 0.0
    for i in np.argsort(-y, kind="stable"):
        if cum < 0.75 * y.sum() or (out and y[i] == y[out[-1]]):
            out.append(int(i)); cum += y[i]
        else:
            break
    return sorted(out)

# Guards: the functions here give the same Gini and Season75 as the saved dataset.
g_saved = df[~monthly].set_index(KEY_SERIES)["Gini"].reindex(wide.index)[volume_ok]
assert np.allclose([gini(r) for r in wide[volume_ok].to_numpy()], g_saved, atol=1e-4)
s75_all = df[monthly].groupby(KEY_SERIES, observed=True)["Season75"].first()
chk75 = wide.dropna()
chk75 = chk75[s75_all.reindex(chk75.index).notna().to_numpy()]     # Latvija 2024 Foreign/Total: broken source series, no Season75
assert all(len(top75(r)) == s for r, s in zip(chk75.to_numpy(), s75_all.reindex(chk75.index))), "top75 differs from Season75"

# Chart style: colours (validated for colour-blind readers) and a helper that gives every chart the same light look.
INK, MUTED, GRIDC = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#e4e3df"
COLOR = {"Domestic": "#2a78d6", "Foreign": "#eb6834", "Total": "#1baf7a"}
PATTERN_COLOR = dict(zip(PATTERNS, ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4"]))
# Months-to-75% classes and foreign-volume classes of the page's map key (same colours as the page).
MCLASSES = ["≤5 months", "6–7 months", "8–9 months"]
MCOLOR = dict(zip(MCLASSES, ["#a94e41", "#ffa91d", "#5c95c4"]))
SIZES = ["<300k", "0.3–3M", ">3M"]
def mclass(m):
    return pd.Categorical(pd.cut(m, [0, 5, 7, 12], labels=MCLASSES), categories=MCLASSES, ordered=True)
def sclass(v):
    return pd.Categorical(pd.cut(v, [0, 3e5, 3e6, np.inf], labels=SIZES, right=False), categories=SIZES, ordered=True)

def style(ax, title, ylabel=None):
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", color=INK, fontsize=12)
    if ylabel:
        ax.set_ylabel(ylabel, color=MUTED)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines[["left", "bottom"]].set_color(MUTED)
    ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
    ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRIDC, lw=0.8)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)

def dumbbell(data, left, right, styles, xlim, xlabel, title):
    """Dot chart, one row per index entry: a grey line from column `left` to column `right` and a dot
    at each end (styles = the scatter settings of the left and the right dot)."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8), dpi=110)
    y_ = np.arange(len(data))
    ax.hlines(y_, data[left], data[right], color=GRIDC, lw=2, zorder=1)
    for col, kw in zip((left, right), styles):
        ax.scatter(data[col], y_, **kw)
    ax.set_yticks(y_, data.index.astype(str)); ax.set_xlim(*xlim)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel, color=MUTED)
    style(ax, title)
    ax.grid(axis="x", color=GRIDC, lw=0.8); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
    return ax

# Region outlines for maps: the projected NUTS 2 polygons embedded in the page (index.html), so the notebook's
# maps show exactly what the page shows. Paths use only M / L / Z; y runs downwards (SVG), so the axis is inverted.
from matplotlib.collections import PathCollection
from matplotlib.patches import Patch, Rectangle
from matplotlib.path import Path
_svg = open("index.html", encoding="utf-8").read()
_svg = _svg[_svg.index('<svg id="map"'):]; _svg = _svg[:_svg.index("</svg>")]
def _svg_path(d):
    verts, codes = [], []
    for ring in re.findall(r"M([^MZ]+)Z?", d):
        pts = [tuple(map(float, p.split(","))) for p in ring.split("L")]
        verts += pts + [pts[0]]; codes += [Path.MOVETO] + [Path.LINETO] * (len(pts) - 1) + [Path.CLOSEPOLY]
    return Path(verts, codes)
_grp = lambda cls: re.search(rf'<g class="{cls}">(.*?)</g>', _svg, re.S).group(1)
MAP_LAND = [_svg_path(d) for d in re.findall(r' d="([^"]+)"', _grp("land"))]
MAP_BORDERS = [_svg_path(d) for d in re.findall(r' d="([^"]+)"', _grp("borders"))]
MAP_REGIONS = [(i, _svg_path(d)) for i, d in re.findall(r'<path class="r" data-id="([^"]+)" d="([^"]+)"', _svg)]
MAP_INSETS = [tuple(float(v) for v in m) for m in re.findall(r'<rect class="inset" x="([\d.]+)" y="([\d.]+)" width="([\d.]+)" height="([\d.]+)"', _svg)]

def region_map(colors, legend, title, note=None):
    """Choropleth of NUTS 2 regions. colors: NUTSCode -> colour; legend: list of (label, colour)."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 8.4), dpi=110)
    for x, y, w, h in MAP_INSETS:
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y), w, h, facecolor="white", edgecolor="#dddee4", lw=0.8, zorder=0))
    ax.add_collection(PathCollection(MAP_LAND, facecolor="#f4f4f4", edgecolor="white", lw=0.3, zorder=1))
    ids = [i for i, _ in MAP_REGIONS]
    ax.add_collection(PathCollection([p for _, p in MAP_REGIONS], facecolor=[colors.get(i, "#b7bbc4") for i in ids],
                                     edgecolor="white", lw=0.25, zorder=2))
    ax.add_collection(PathCollection(MAP_BORDERS, facecolor="none", edgecolor="white", lw=0.9, zorder=3))
    ax.set_xlim(0, 508); ax.set_ylim(600, 0); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", color=INK, fontsize=11)
    ax.legend(handles=[Patch(facecolor=c, edgecolor="none", label=l) for l, c in legend], frameon=False, fontsize=8,
              loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 0.89), title=note, title_fontsize=8, alignment="left")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    unmapped = sorted(set(colors) - set(ids))
    print(f"{len(ids)} regions mapped; not mapped (overseas, Azores, Madeira and similar):", len(unmapped))

# Annual rows of one NUTS level (and year, guest group), with Season75 taken from the monthly rows.
ann_all = df[~monthly].drop(columns="Season75").join(s75_all, on=KEY_SERIES)
def annual(level, year=None, residence="Foreign"):
    a = ann_all[(ann_all["NUTSLevel"] == level) & (ann_all["ResidenceCountry"] == residence)]
    if year is not None:
        a = a[a["Year"] == year]
    return a

fo = annual(2, 2025).set_index("NUTSCode")                          # NUTS 2 regions, 2025, foreign guests
fo = fo.assign(mclass=mclass(fo["Season75"]), size=sclass(fo["Value"]))
fok = fo[fo["VolumeOK"] == 1]                                      # ... with enough foreign nights for the indices
cty = annual(0, 2025).set_index("Country")                          # countries, 2025, foreign guests
EFTA = ["Iceland", "Liechtenstein", "Norway", "Switzerland"]
EU27 = [c for c in COUNTRIES if c not in EFTA]
ann_t = annual(2, 2025, "Total")                                    # NUTS 2 regions, 2025, all guests (Parts 1 and 4.1)
ok_t = ann_t[ann_t["VolumeOK"] == 1]                                # ... with enough nights for seasonality indices
cty_t = annual(0, 2025, "Total")                                    # countries, 2025, all guests
GEO_SHARES = ["PrcCoastal", "PrcRural", "PrcIsland", "PrcInlandMountain"]
geo = annual(2, 2025, "Total").set_index("NUTSCode")[GEO_SHARES + ["PrcForeign", "ForeignGroup"]]  # region attributes
print(f"{len(df):,} rows; {len(fo)} NUTS 2 regions, {len(fok)} with enough foreign nights for seasonality indices; "
      f"{len(cty)} countries")

118,794 rows; 259 NUTS 2 regions, 255 with enough foreign nights for seasonality indices; 31 countries

1. Foreign tourism in context¶

Preliminary to the foreign-guest analysis; not on the page. This part looks at all guests and at the foreign share of nights: how foreign stays developed since 2019 and where they are, before sections 2–5 turn to foreign guests' seasons. The foreign share and the foreign groups (Mainly domestic < 40%, Mixed, Mainly foreign ≥ 70%) are defined in the indices notebook, A5.

1.1 Foreign stays collapsed with COVID; since 2019 domestic stays grew faster in % terms, foreign stays more in absolute nights¶

EU-27 totals (sum of the 27 country rows). The foreign share of nights was 67% in 2019, fell to 42% in 2020 and has been stable at 62% since 2023: foreign stays recovered fully, but domestic stays grew faster (+112% against +73% since 2019).

1.2 Foreign guests are the majority almost everywhere, and concentrated in a few large regions¶

  • Countries: the foreign share ranges from 29% in Germany, 39% in Poland and 40% in France to over 95% in Malta, Iceland and Liechtenstein; the median country is 73% foreign. Since 2019 it fell in 26 of 31 countries — by more than 5 points in 13 (Lithuania, Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Czechia most) — because domestic platform stays grew faster (1.1).
  • Regions: 79 of 259 NUTS 2 regions are mainly foreign (≥ 70%); they have 48% of all nights and 64% of all foreign nights. The 10 regions with the most foreign nights — the Croatian coast, Andalucía, Canarias, Île de France, Cataluña, Valencia, Lazio, Provence, Lombardia, Toscana — hold 36% of them (of 606.8 million foreign nights in all 259 NUTS 2 regions, EU and EFTA; table, last column). Since 2019 the foreign share fell in 74% of regions (median −2.5 points).
  • Whether depending on foreign guests makes a region more seasonal is section 4.1.

2. Where and when do foreign guests stay?¶

Page: the map (colour = months to 75%, shade = foreign nights), the country-by-month grid and the four notes.

2.1 609 million foreign nights, in the map's three volume classes¶

  • Volume. Foreign guests spent 609.4 million nights in the 31 countries in 2025 — 62% of all platform-booked nights. The 259 NUTS 2 regions add up to 606.8 million (0.4% less than the country totals; the page's headline uses the country total). How this changed since 2019 is in 1.1.
  • The map's three volume classes. 43 regions have over 3 million foreign nights and hold 73% of them; 149 have 0.3–3 million (25%); 67 have fewer than 300,000 (2%). The ten largest hold 36% (1.2).
  • Because the map shades regions by volume, its darkest cells carry most of the foreign nights while many regions on it are small; the key on the page counts regions, not nights (2.3 gives both).
  • Map (volume alone, five classes nested in the page's three). The regions over 3 million are the Mediterranean coasts and islands (Spain, southern France, Italy, the Croatian coast, Greece, Malta, Cyprus), the big capitals (Paris, Madrid, Lisbon, Lazio, Budapest, Vienna, Prague, Athens) and the Alps (Tirol, Salzburg, Rhône-Alpes). The smallest (under 100,000) are inland regions of Poland, Romania, Bulgaria and northern Greece and very small territories (Ceuta, Melilla, Mayotte, Åland, Liechtenstein). As on the page, 8 regions outside the map frame (overseas regions, Azores, Madeira) are counted but not drawn.

2.2 Summer carries the year¶

  • 44% of all foreign nights fall in June–August (31 countries). Foreign nights are spread evenly over July and August; compared with domestic guests, more of them fall in June and September and fewer in August and December (chart).
  • In 30 of 31 countries the busiest month for foreign guests is in June–August — August in 23, July in 7. The exception is Finland, which peaks in December (Lapland).

2.3 Months to reach 75% of foreign nights: from 3 on the Croatian coast to 9 in the capitals¶

The measure (Season75, indices notebook A1): the busiest months that together hold three-quarters of a region's foreign nights. An evenly spread year needs 9; a single-month year would need 1. Fewer months = a more concentrated season. The page colours it in three classes: ≤ 5 months (short season), 6–7, 8–9 (an almost even year).

  • Distribution. The typical (median) region needs 7 months. 40 regions need 5 or fewer, 123 need 6–7, 96 need 8–9. No country needs 9: national totals mix seasonal and year-round regions.
  • The map key (regions × volume). By regions the largest cell is 6–7 months × 0.3–3M (72 regions). By nights it is 6–7 months × > 3M (29% of foreign nights) and 8–9 × > 3M (27%): the large year-round cities. The 10 regions with a short season and over 3 million foreign nights hold 17% of all foreign nights (2.5).
  • Map (months to 75% alone). Short seasons (darkest, ≤ 5 months) line the Adriatic and almost all of Greece (every Greek region except Attiki and Dytiki Makedonia), the French Atlantic coast and Corsica, the Bulgarian Black Sea coast and Lake Balaton, and Scandinavia's summer-cottage and fjord regions (Småland, Västsverige, Innlandet, Vestlandet, Åland); Finnish Lapland's five months are its winter. Almost-even years (lightest, 8–9) cover most of Germany, Poland and Czechia, the capitals, and much of Spain (Madrid, Andalucía, Valencia, Canarias). The 6–7-month middle tones are the rest: Italy, inland France, Portugal, the Baltic states.
  • The page's notes, checked (table below):
    • The coast is all-or-nothing: Croatia needs 4 months (June–September), its coast (Jadranska Hrvatska) 3, and the coast has 95% of Croatia's foreign nights. Greece and Slovenia need 5.
    • Cities keep the lights on: Madrid, Budapest, Berlin, Brussels and Bucharest need 9. They are not the only ones: 15 regions need 9, among them Sofia's region (Yugozapaden) and several German city regions (Stuttgart, Frankfurt's Darmstadt, Düsseldorf, Leipzig).
    • Winter is the other season: Austria and Finland are the only countries whose 75% months include five of the six months November–April; Canarias' busiest month for foreign guests is January.

2.4 How to read months to 75%¶

  • It ranks regions like the Gini index. Across the 255 regions with enough foreign nights the rank correlation with the Gini index of foreign nights is −0.96 (fewer months = higher Gini). The page uses months to 75% for the map because it can be said in one sentence, and the Gini index for the seasonality rank in the profiles (the Seasonality tile).
  • It is stable. From 2024 to 2025, 87% of regions keep the same number of months, 99% move by at most one, and 94% stay in the same colour class (89% through 2023–2025). A one-month difference between two regions is within normal movement; a class difference mostly is not.
  • It ignores the calendar order. A region with a winter and a summer season can need as many months as a region with one long season: Tirol needs 7, Salzburg 6, Rhône-Alpes 7 — the map shows them in the middle class. The patterns in section 3 separate them.

        "same class 2024-2025": (cls_y[2024] == cls_y[2025]).mean(),
        "same class 2023, 2024 and 2025": ((cls_y[2023] == cls_y[2025]) & (cls_y[2024] == cls_y[2025])).mean()}
print(f"stability of Season75, {len(s75_y)} regions:")
display(pd.Series(stab).mul(100).round(0).to_frame("% of regions"))

2.5 Volume and season length are separate dimensions¶

The map's two dimensions — how many foreign nights, and how concentrated — are only loosely related, so both are needed:

  • Across regions larger destinations are slightly more seasonal (rank correlation between foreign nights and months to 75%: −0.20). The share of short-season regions (≤ 5 months) rises from 4% among regions under 300,000 foreign nights to 23% among those over 3 million, but the median is 7–8 months in every class.
  • Within countries the link disappears (0.02): a country's big regions are not its seasonal ones. The cross-country link comes from Croatia and Greece, which are both large and seasonal. Section 5 confirms that volume adds nothing once geography and country are known.
  • Big and short — the map's darkest red cell (≤ 5 months, > 3 million foreign nights): 10 regions with 17% of all foreign nights — the Croatian coast, Provence, Kriti, Notio Aigaio, Ionia Nisia, Sardegna, Kentriki Makedonia, Aquitaine, Zahodna Slovenija, Bretagne. These are where the most foreign nights depend on the shortest season.

3. What seasonal cycles are there?¶

Page: chapter 2, the five patterns of foreign demand.

3.1 Five patterns of foreign demand¶

Each region's foreign nights get one of five patterns from their monthly profile (indices notebook, A7); only the 255 regions with at least 10,000 foreign nights are classified. Ordered from the most to the least seasonal:

Pattern Regions Months to 75% (average profile) Seasonality score S_R (median) Largest regions Typical geography (vs all 255)
Strong summer season 58 5 0.47 Croatian coast, Provence, Kriti coastal 1.6 ×, rural 1.9 ×
Summer season 131 7 0.25 Andalucía, Cataluña, Valencia none stands out
Summer season + winter shoulder 5 8 0.18 Région lémanique, Trento, Norra Mellansverige mountain 3.9 ×
Winter-based seasons 18 7 0.15 Rhône-Alpes, Tirol, Salzburg mountain 4 ×
Mild or no season 43 9 0.12 Canarias, Île de France, Lazio urban 2.3 ×
  • Typical geography = how much more often the pattern's regions are predominantly coastal, island, inland mountain, rural (≥ 50% of residents) or urban (≤ 20% rural) than all 255 regions; the page shows a type when it is at least 1.6 × as common.
  • Firmness. Four patterns are stable: 86–93% of their regions keep the pattern through 2023–2025. Summer season + winter shoulder is not: only 1 of its 5 regions keeps it (the page marks it as a small group).
  • The ordering by S_R (calendar-aware, section 3.2) differs from the ordering by months to 75%: winter-based regions need 7 months but have a low S_R because their two seasons fill each other's off-season.
In [11]:
# Seasonal factors (month / average month) of every reliable foreign series; average profile of each pattern, 2025.
fac = wide[volume_ok].div(wide[volume_ok].sum(axis=1), axis=0) * T
pat_codes = {p: fok.index[fok["SeasonPattern"] == p] for p in PATTERNS}
prof_pat = pd.DataFrame({p: fac.loc[[(c_, 2025, "Foreign") for c_ in codes]].mean() for p, codes in pat_codes.items()}).T
sr_f = pd.Series({c_: s_r(wide.loc[(c_, 2025, "Foreign")]) for c_ in fok.index})
GEO_TYPES = {"coastal": geo["PrcCoastal"] >= 50, "island": geo["PrcIsland"] >= 50, "inland mountain": geo["PrcInlandMountain"] >= 50,
             "rural": geo["PrcRural"] >= 50, "urban": geo["PrcRural"] <= 20}
base = {g: s.reindex(fok.index).mean() for g, s in GEO_TYPES.items()}
pat_tab = pd.DataFrame({p: {
    "regions": len(codes),
    "months to 75% (average profile)": len(top75(prof_pat.loc[p])),
    "S_R median": round(sr_f[codes].median(), 2),
    "largest regions": ", ".join(fok.loc[codes].nlargest(3, "Value")["Region"]),
    **{f"{g} ×": round(s.reindex(codes).mean() / base[g], 1) for g, s in GEO_TYPES.items()}} for p, codes in pat_codes.items()}).T
display(pat_tab)
print("share of regions of each type among all 255, %:", {g: round(100 * v) for g, v in base.items()})

# Firmness: does a region keep its 2025 pattern in 2023 and 2024?
pp = annual(2).pivot_table(index="NUTSCode", columns="Year", values="SeasonPattern", aggfunc="first", observed=True)[[2023, 2024, 2025]].dropna()
keep_ = ((pp[2023] == pp[2025]) & (pp[2024] == pp[2025])).groupby(pp[2025], observed=True).agg(["size", "mean"])
keep_.columns = ["regions (data 2023-25)", "% keeping the pattern"]
display(keep_.assign(**{"% keeping the pattern": lambda d: (100 * d["% keeping the pattern"]).round(0)}).reindex(PATTERNS))

3.2 Two-season regions: why the page scores patterns with S_R¶

Months to 75% and the Gini index ignore the order of the months, so they rate a winter-and-summer region like a region with one season of the same total length. S_R (Lo Magno, Ferrante & De Cantis 2017) measures how far nights would have to move around the calendar to even out the year, so two seasons that fill each other's off-season score lower. The two measures agree for almost all regions and part only for the 12 two-season regions — all Alpine, Nordic or Central European ski-and-summer regions, all in the Winter-based seasons pattern (chart). This is why the page's pattern chapter shows S_R as the Seasonality score.

3.3 Countries: Croatia, Greece and Slovenia have the most seasonal foreign demand¶

The page's country profiles rank the 31 countries by the Gini index of their foreign nights (the Seasonality tile: 1 = most seasonal). Croatia, Greece and Slovenia lead, as on the months-to-75% grid. The least seasonal foreign demand is in Luxembourg, Czechia, Spain, Hungary and Germany: city-break countries, and Spain, where winter-peaking Canarias and year-round Madrid offset the summer coasts.

4. Do foreign guests sharpen the local tourist season?¶

Page: chapter 3, the three effect classes and the region profiles' "Foreign guests' year".

Four questions, answered in turn:

  • 4.1 Are regions that depend on foreign guests more seasonal? — Not in general, and nothing in the data suggests that foreign dependency causes seasonality.
  • 4.2 How much does foreign guests' timing add to a region's seasonality? — Little in the typical region, a lot where they dominate.
  • 4.3 What do the three effect classes look like?
  • 4.4 Why? — Foreign guests are the more summer-concentrated group in most regions; where domestic guests crowd into August, foreign guests smooth the year.

4.1 Foreign dependency is not the same as seasonality, and the data show no causal link¶

Foreign share does not tell you how seasonal a region is. Mainly-foreign regions include both the most seasonal places (the Croatian coast, the Greek islands) and the least seasonal (Paris, Madrid, Canarias). All guests, Gini index of all nights, NUTS 2 regions with enough nights, 2025.

  • Across regions the link is weak: rank correlation 0.14. Because regions of the same country are not independent, its 95% interval is computed by resampling whole countries: −0.10 to 0.30, which includes zero.
  • Across countries it is also weak: 0.19, not significant (p = 0.31).
  • Within countries it is slightly negative (−0.19, more than chance: p < 0.01): a country's more foreign regions tend to be its less seasonal ones — mostly capitals and cities. This is strongest in Belgium, Romania, Denmark, Portugal, Germany and Italy; Greece and the Netherlands go the other way (table below).
  • Once geography and country are known, foreign share adds nothing (5.2): the within-country pattern reflects cities attracting foreign guests, the cross-country pattern Croatia and Greece being both very foreign and very seasonal.

No causal link. Nothing in these data indicates that depending on foreign guests makes a region seasonal. The association is weak across regions, not significant across countries, slightly negative within countries, and it disappears once geography and country are accounted for. Where foreign-heavy regions are seasonal, both follow from where they are: coasts and islands attract foreign guests and have short summers. These are observational data, so they cannot prove that no effect exists — but they give no support for one. Whether foreign guests' timing adds to a region's seasonality is a different question (4.2–4.4), and that answer, too, is an accounting comparison, not a causal effect.

Double exposure — mainly foreign (≥ 70%) and a high Gini index (≥ 0.30): about 30 regions with about a fifth of all nights — the Croatian coast, Greek islands, Balearics, Algarve, Sicilia, Toscana, Veneto. They depend on foreign guests and on a short season, so they are the most exposed to a change in foreign demand, even though the one does not cause the other. The size of this group depends on its cut-offs: with the Gini cut 0.02 lower or higher and the foreign cut 5 points lower or higher, it holds 16–45 regions and 13–27% of nights (table below). Its foreign-guest counterpart on the page is big and short (2.5).

# Regions of one country are not independent: resample whole countries (bootstrap) for an honest 95% interval.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
oc_t = ok_t["Country"].astype(str)
pos_c = {c_: np.flatnonzero(oc_t == c_) for c_ in oc_t.unique()}         # row positions of each country
boot = [rk(ok_t.iloc[np.concatenate([pos_c[c_] for c_ in rng.choice(oc_t.unique(), oc_t.nunique())])]) for _ in range(1000)]
boot_ci = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])

# Within countries: correlation of ranks after removing each country's average rank (countries with 3+ regions).

# Is it more than chance? Shuffle the Gini ranks within each country and recompute (2,000 times).

    g = rG_dm.copy()
    for ix in pos_w:

4.2 Foreign timing sharpens the year in 105 regions and smooths it in 27 — but the typical effect is small¶

The measure — ForeignTimingEffect (indices notebook, A6): the Gini index of all the region's nights minus the Gini it would have if foreign guests kept their number of nights but travelled in the same months as its domestic guests. Because the Gini index does not depend on scale, that second Gini is simply the Gini of domestic nights alone. Classes: sharpens (above +0.03), smooths (below −0.03), no clear effect in between (0.03 is the upper end of normal year-to-year movement). It is an accounting comparison, not a causal effect. Regions: the 254 with at least 10,000 nights from each group (Ceuta, Melilla, Mayotte and Liechtenstein fall short on one side; Mount Athos on both).

  • Classes. Sharper in 105 of 254 regions (41%), flatter in 27 (11%), no clear difference in 122.
  • Size. If foreign guests travelled in the same months as domestic guests, the typical (median) region's Gini would be about 0.015 lower — within normal year-to-year movement. By foreign share: about 0 where foreign guests are under 40% of nights, 0.02 at 40–70%, 0.06 where they are 70% or more (77 regions; chart, left). For the EU-27 as a whole: 0.261 instead of 0.241.
  • Largest values. The largest sharpening effects are in regions where foreign guests are 84–95% of nights (Kentriki Makedonia, Anatoliki Makedonia, Zahodna Slovenija). There the "domestic pattern" is borrowed from a small group, so read them as "foreign and domestic timing differ strongly", not as precise amounts.
  • Over time (the same 237 regions every year): outside COVID the median effect is 0.006–0.014 and foreign timing sharpens the year in 38–41% of regions — no trend. In 2020–21 it was around zero and foreign timing smoothed the year in 24–27% of regions (chart, right).

4.3 What the three classes look like¶

The page draws, for each class, the average year of all guests and of domestic guests (seasonal factors averaged over the class's regions), and the months-to-75% squares of a typical region (the class's median Season75; the squares are that many busiest months of the average profile).

  • Sharpens (105 regions — the Croatian coast, Île de France, Provence, Lombardia, Toscana). Domestic demand is fairly even; foreign guests pile into July–August. All guests together need fewer months to reach 75% than domestic guests alone in 72 of the 105 regions, never more. Strongest: Kentriki Makedonia, July–August at 2.76 × an average month for all guests against 1.39 × for domestic guests.
  • No clear effect (122 — Cataluña, Lazio, Illes Balears, Rhône-Alpes, Madrid). Both groups share much the same year; in 103 of the 122 regions all guests need the same number of months as domestic guests.
  • Smooths (27 — Andalucía, Canarias, Valencia, Algarve, Sicilia). Domestic guests crowd into July–August; foreign guests fill spring and autumn. All guests need more months than domestic guests in 16 of the 27, never fewer. Strongest: Algarve, July–August at 2.32 × for all guests against 3.39 × for domestic guests.

4.4 Why: which group crowds into the summer¶

  • Foreign guests are the more seasonal group in about three-quarters of regions. In 2025 their own Gini index is higher than domestic guests' in 76% of NUTS 2 regions (by more than 0.03 in 63%; domestic guests are clearly more seasonal in 17%). Nationally this is recent: 24 of 30 countries in 2025, 53–67% in 2018–2024. The exceptions are Spain, Portugal, Cyprus, Hungary, Germany and Czechia (chart).
  • Which group has the sharper July–August peak decides the direction. The peak = July–August nights per average month; "much sharper" = more than 0.25 apart:
July–August peak Smooths No clear effect Sharpens Regions
domestic peak much sharper 49% 43% 8% 37
foreign peak much sharper 2% 30% 67% 125

In between (peaks less than 0.25 apart; 92 regions) the effect is mostly too small to tell from zero.

  • Where foreign guests smooth the year — Spain's and southern Italy's coasts and islands and the Algarve — they fill the shoulder months (in Canarias the winter) that domestic guests leave empty. This holds even in mainly-foreign regions (10 of 77). Nationally the same holds in Hungary, Cyprus, Spain, Czechia and Portugal; in Germany domestic guests are also more seasonal, but with 29% foreign nights the effect stays small.

5. What explains seasonality?¶

Page: the "Typical geography" row of chapter 2. Not otherwise on the page.

5.1 Geography, not volume, explains the length of the foreign season¶

Is a region's foreign season short because of where it is, or because it is a big foreign destination (the map's second dimension)? Regression of each region's months to 75% (2025, 254 regions with enough foreign nights and geography data) on its foreign nights (log₁₀, so the coefficient is per tenfold more nights), the four geography shares (coefficient = change from 0% to 100%) and, in the last models, country effects; standard errors clustered by country. The Gini index of foreign nights gives the same picture (second table).

Model Volume, ×10 foreign nights (months) p Coastal 0→100% Rural 0→100% R²
volume only −0.37 0.12 0.03
+ geography −0.42 0.08 −1.6 −3.7 0.38
+ geography + country −0.33 0.21 −1.3 −3.7 0.56
geography + country, no volume −1.4 −3.2 0.55
  • Geography holds in every model. A fully rural region needs about 3–4 fewer months to reach 75% of its foreign nights than a fully urban one; a fully coastal region about 1.3–1.6 fewer than an inland one. Islands and inland mountains add nothing beyond that.
  • Volume adds nothing. On its own it explains 3% of the differences; with geography and country it is not significant, and adding it to geography and country raises R² only from 0.55 to 0.56.

So where a region is (coast, countryside, country) shapes how long its foreign season is; how many foreign guests it has does not, once that is known. The two dimensions of the map are separate. Not in the data, and so not tested: guests' countries of origin, climate, airport access, ski infrastructure and accommodation supply.

def ols_cluster(y, X, groups):
    """OLS coefficients with country-clustered standard errors (CR1, as in Stata / statsmodels)
    and p-values from a t distribution with (number of countries - 1) degrees of freedom."""
    y, X = np.asarray(y, float), np.asarray(X, float)
    XtX_inv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X); b = XtX_inv @ X.T @ y; u = y - X @ b
    g_codes = pd.factorize(np.asarray(groups))[0]; G = g_codes.max() + 1; n, k = X.shape
    meat = sum(np.outer(X[g_codes == g].T @ u[g_codes == g], X[g_codes == g].T @ u[g_codes == g]) for g in range(G))
    se = np.sqrt(np.diag(XtX_inv @ meat @ XtX_inv) * G / (G - 1) * (n - 1) / (n - k))
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(np.abs(b / se), G - 1)
    r2 = 1 - (u @ u) / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    return b, se, p, r2

5.2 Foreign share adds nothing once geography and country are known¶

4.1 shows that foreign share and seasonality are only loosely related; 5.1 that geography matters. Are foreign guests a separate factor, or do they simply go where the seasonal places are? Regression of each NUTS 2 region's Gini index of all nights (2025) on its foreign share, step by step adding the four geography shares and country effects (standard errors clustered by country):

Model Foreign share, 0 → 100% (change in Gini) p R²
Foreign share only +0.09 0.16 0.03
+ geography +0.10 0.008 0.42
+ geography + country +0.04 0.58 0.55
same, weighted by nights −0.06 0.39
  • On its own, foreign share explains 3% of the differences in seasonality between regions.
  • With geography it looks significant — but only because it then picks up differences between countries: Croatia and Greece are both very foreign and very seasonal. Within countries (country effects added) it adds nothing (R² 0.544 → 0.546), and among the large regions (weighted by nights) the sign even turns negative.
  • Geography holds in every model: from 0% to 100% coastal adds about 0.14–0.16 to the Gini index, from 0% to 100% rural about 0.35.

This is the evidence behind the statement in 4.1: where a region is (coast, countryside, country) shapes its seasonality; who its guests are does not add anything once that is known.

In [19]:
# Gini (all guests) ~ foreign share (+ geography shares) (+ country effects), NUTS 2 regions 2025, clustered by country.
gs_t = ok_t.dropna(subset=GEO_SHARES + ["PrcForeign"])
Zt = gs_t[GEO_SHARES].to_numpy() / 100
Ft = gs_t[["PrcForeign"]].to_numpy() / 100
ct_t = gs_t["Country"].astype(str)
Dt = pd.get_dummies(ct_t, drop_first=True, dtype=float).to_numpy()
models_t = {"foreign share only": [Ft], "+ geography": [Ft, Zt], "+ geography + country": [Ft, Zt, Dt],
            "geography + country (no foreign)": [Zt, Dt]}
rows_t, FIT_T = {}, {}
for name, parts in models_t.items():
    Xr = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(gs_t))] + parts)
    b_, se_, p_, r2_ = ols_cluster(gs_t["Gini"], Xr, ct_t)
    FIT_T[name] = (b_, se_, p_, r2_)
    has_f = parts[0] is Ft
    row = {"foreign share (0->100%)": f"{b_[1]:+.3f} ± {se_[1]:.3f} (p {p_[1]:.3f})" if has_f else "—"}
    off = 1 if has_f else 0
    if any(part is Zt for part in parts):
        row |= {k: f"{b_[1 + off + j]:+.3f} ± {se_[1 + off + j]:.3f}" for j, k in enumerate(["coastal", "rural", "island", "inland mountain"])}
    rows_t[name] = row | {"R²": round(r2_, 3)}
print(f"Gini of all nights, {len(gs_t)} NUTS 2 regions 2025; coefficient ± clustered standard error:")
cols_t = ["foreign share (0->100%)", "coastal", "rural", "island", "inland mountain", "R²"]
display(pd.DataFrame(rows_t).T.reindex(columns=cols_t).astype(object).where(lambda d: d.notna(), ""))
# Weighted by nights: do the large tourism regions tell a different story?
Xw = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(gs_t)), Ft, Zt, Dt]); sw = np.sqrt(gs_t["Value"].to_numpy(float))
bw, sew, pw, _ = ols_cluster(gs_t["Gini"].to_numpy() * sw, Xw * sw[:, None], ct_t)
print(f"weighted by nights, + geography + country: foreign share {bw[1]:+.3f} ± {sew[1]:.3f} (p {pw[1]:.2f})")

Conclusions¶

  1. Context: foreign guests are the majority of platform-booked nights almost everywhere (62% EU-wide), but their share is slowly falling as domestic platform stays grow faster, and their nights are concentrated in a few large regions.
  2. Foreign tourism — 609 million platform-booked nights in 2025 — is concentrated in space and time: the 43 largest regions hold almost three-quarters of the nights, and 44% of them fall in June–August.
  3. Season length ranges from 3 months to reach 75% of the year's foreign nights on the Croatian coast to 9 in the capitals and several German city regions; the typical region needs 7. Winter is a second season only in the Alps, the Nordic ski regions and Canarias.
  4. Five patterns describe foreign demand: strong summer (coast, countryside), summer (everywhere), winter-based (mountains), mild or no season (cities), and a small, unstable summer-plus-winter-shoulder group. Two-season regions look mid-seasonal on months to 75%; the calendar-aware S_R shows them as among the least seasonal.
  5. Foreign guests sharpen the year where they are more summer-concentrated than domestic guests (105 regions) and smooth it where domestic guests crowd into August (27, mainly Spain's coasts, Algarve, Sicilia). The effect is small in the typical region and about 0.06 Gini where foreign guests dominate.
  6. Foreign dependency does not cause seasonality. A region's foreign share is only loosely related to how seasonal it is (rank correlation 0.14, slightly negative within countries) and adds nothing once geography and country are known. The data give no support for a causal link: foreign-heavy seasonal regions (the double exposure group) are seasonal because of where they are, not because their guests are foreign.
  7. Where, not how big: geography and country explain the length of the foreign season; foreign volume adds nothing. The map's two dimensions are separate — and the 10 big and short regions (17% of foreign nights; the Croatian coast, Provence, the Greek islands, Sardegna, the French Atlantic) are where the most foreign nights depend on the shortest season.

Limitations¶

  • Platform bookings only (Airbnb, Booking, Expedia, Tripadvisor): hotels booked directly and most domestic holiday homes are missing; growth since 2019 partly reflects wider platform use.
  • Foreign guests are one group — the data give no countries of origin, so the role of individual source markets (e.g. Northern Europeans in the shoulder months) cannot be tested.
  • Mostly a 2025 snapshot. Months to 75% is stable from year to year (2.4), but changes of one month are within normal movement. Dutch and Portuguese NUTS 2 regions start in 2024.
  • Months to 75% and the Gini index ignore the calendar order (two-season regions, 3.2), and months to 75% is a whole number, so close regions can fall either side of a class border.
  • Geography shares describe residents, not where guests stay; climate, airport access, ski infrastructure, accommodation supply and prices are not in the data.
  • Results are associations and accounting comparisons, not causal effects.

chk = pd.DataFrame(CLAIMS, columns=["statement", "computed", "in text", "tolerance"])
chk["ok"] = (chk["computed"].astype(float) - chk["in text"]).abs() <= chk["tolerance"] + 1e-9
print(f"{chk['ok'].sum()} of {len(chk)} quoted numbers match the data")
display(chk[~chk["ok"]] if not chk["ok"].all() else chk.round(4))
assert chk["ok"].all(), "numbers quoted in the text no longer match the data - update the statements listed above"

Appendix B — Does the page match the data?¶

index.html embeds its data (DATA: one record per country and region; PAT: the five pattern profiles; the three effect-class profiles in chapter 3) and states numbers in its text. This cell reads the page and checks every embedded field and the key numbers against the dataset and the calculations above. Re-run it after rebuilding the page.

In [21]:
html = open("index.html", encoding="utf-8").read()
grab = lambda name, open_, close_: json.loads(re.search(rf"var {name} = (\{open_}.*?\{close_});\n", html).group(1))
DATA, PAT = grab("DATA", "{", "}"), grab("PAT", "[", "]")
f25 = lambda c_, res: (c_, 2025, res)                # key of a 2025 series
row = ann_all[ann_all["Year"] == 2025].set_index(["NUTSCode", "ResidenceCountry"])
bad = []
for k, d in DATA.items():
    f_, t_, dm_ = row.loc[(k, "Foreign")], row.loc[(k, "Total")], row.loc[(k, "Domestic")]
    tests = {
        "f (monthly foreign nights)": list(wide.loc[f25(k, "Foreign")].astype(int)) == d["f"],
        "d (monthly domestic nights)": d["d"] is None or list(wide.loc[f25(k, "Domestic")].astype(int)) == d["d"],
        "fm = Season75 foreign": d["fm"] == f_["Season75"],
        "fs = Prc75Flag foreign": list(flags.loc[f25(k, "Foreign")].astype(int)) == d["fs"],
        "dm = Season75 domestic": d["dm"] is None or d["dm"] == dm_["Season75"],
        "fok / dok = VolumeOK": d["fok"] == f_["VolumeOK"] and d["dok"] == dm_["VolumeOK"],
        "fp = SeasonPattern foreign": (d["fp"] or None) == (f_["SeasonPattern"] if pd.notna(f_["SeasonPattern"]) else None),
        "fpc = SeasonalityPercentile": (d["fpc"] is None) == pd.isna(f_["SeasonalityPercentile"]) and (d["fpc"] is None or d["fpc"] == f_["SeasonalityPercentile"]),
        "te = ForeignTimingEffect": (d["te"] is None) == pd.isna(t_["ForeignTimingEffect"]) and (d["te"] is None or abs(d["te"] - t_["ForeignTimingEffect"]) < 6e-4),
        "tc = ForeignTimingClass": (d["tc"] or None) == (t_["ForeignTimingClass"] if pd.notna(t_["ForeignTimingClass"]) else None),
        "geography shares": d["co"] is None or all(d[a] is None or abs(d[a] - t_[b]) <= 0.5 for a, b in
                                                   [("co", "PrcCoastal"), ("ci", "PrcCities"), ("ru", "PrcRural"), ("mo", "PrcInlandMountain"), ("is", "PrcIsland")])}
    bad += [(k, t) for t, ok_ in tests.items() if not ok_]
print(f"DATA: {len(DATA)} records ({sum(d['l'] == 0 for d in DATA.values())} countries, {sum(d['l'] == 2 for d in DATA.values())} regions); "
      f"{len(bad)} field mismatches", bad[:10])

# Pattern profiles (chapter 2) and effect-class profiles (chapter 3).
pat_ok = all(p["n"] == pat_n[p["name"]] and np.allclose(p["prof"], prof_pat.loc[p["name"]].round(2))
             and [e.rsplit(" (", 1)[0] for e in p["ex"]] == pat_tab.loc[p["name"], "largest regions"].split(", ") for p in PAT)
EP_JS = {m.group(1): {"d": json.loads(m.group(2)), "t": json.loads(m.group(3)), "m": json.loads(m.group(4)),
                      "tf": json.loads(m.group(5)), "td": json.loads(m.group(6))}
         for m in re.finditer(r"key: '([^']+)'.*?d: (\[[^\]]+\]), t: (\[[^\]]+\]).*?m: (\[[^\]]+\]), tf: (\[[^\]]+\]), td: (\[[^\]]+\])", html, re.S)}
sq = lambda idx: [int(i in idx) for i in range(12)]
ep_ok = {k: (np.allclose(EP_JS[k]["d"], eff[k]["d"]) and np.allclose(EP_JS[k]["t"], eff[k]["t"])
             and EP_JS[k]["m"] == [eff[k]["median months, all guests"], eff[k]["median months, domestic"]]
             and EP_JS[k]["tf"] == sq(eff[k]["squares all"]) and EP_JS[k]["td"] == sq(eff[k]["squares domestic"])) for k in EFF_CLASSES}
print("PAT (patterns) match:", pat_ok, "| effect classes match:", ep_ok)

# Numbers written in the page's text.
TEXT = [("259 regions", "259 regions", len(fo)), ("609M foreign nights", "609M", round(f_cty25)),
        ("44% in June-August", "44% fell in June–August", round(jja)), ("30 of 31 countries", "In 30 of 31 countries", peak_month.isin(["June", "July", "August"]).sum()),
        ("95% on the Adriatic", "95% of its foreign nights", round(hr_coast_share)), ("255 regions with patterns", "255 regions", len(fok)),
        ("105 sharper", "sharper in 105 regions", (cf["ForeignTimingClass"] == "Adds").sum()), ("27 flatter", "flatter in 27", (cf["ForeignTimingClass"] == "Reduces").sum()),
        ("254 regions compared", "254 regions", len(cf)), ("about 0.015", "about 0.015", round(cf["ForeignTimingEffect"].median(), 3)),
        ("about 0.06 at >= 70% foreign", "about 0.06", round(by_fg.loc["Mainly foreign", "median"], 2))]
page_chk = pd.DataFrame([(n, s in html, v) for n, s, v in TEXT], columns=["claim", "phrase on page", "value here"])
display(page_chk)
assert not bad and pat_ok and all(ep_ok.values()) and page_chk["phrase on page"].all(), "the page and the data differ - see above"
